earlier_scan.note: Preliminary: word-final acoustic prominence (pitch) typical, penult prominence in list intonation; stress system still under investigation. (Retired code; source covers Sanapaná [spn])

new_statements.quote: Looking, firstly, at monomorphemic Nouns, pitch seems to be the clearest correlate of acoustic prominence. In bisyllabic Nouns of a variety of syllabic structures, in the overwhelming majority of cases the second syllable is more prominent than the first. Of 47 investigated tokens in isolation (and thus presumably in their citation form), the second syllable has higher pitch at the midpoint of the vowel than the first in 40 cases. [...] [p.157] Nouns in Sanapaná tend to show greatest prominence on their final syllable in isolation, with an additional high-prominence syllable two syllables earlier (i.e. the first and third syllables in three-syllable words, the second and fourth in four-syllable words).

new_statements.rule_in_words: In citation forms the word-final syllable carries the main (pitch-cued) prominence, regardless of syllable structure or morphological make-up (prefix+root, root+plural suffix behave alike); the author explicitly refrains from positing a phonological stress system and calls these preliminary instrumental observations. Independently, Silva Gomes 2013 (UNICAMP diss., fn.32 p.96, pp.128-129) treats stress as falling 'preferencialmente em posição final de palavra', the Sanapaná default, 'definido localmente e não através do tipo silábico' (not weight-driven).
new_statements.secondary_stress: An additional high-pitch syllable two syllables before the final (1st+3rd in trisyllables, 2nd+4th in four-syllable words), i.e. alternating rhythm leftward from the final; the middle syllable of trisyllables has lowest pitch and intensity.
new_statements.exceptions: Initial-syllable prominence occurred in a minority of tokens (7/47 bisyllables, all with closed first syllable; 9/33 trisyllables, no syllable-type correlation), always on the second repetition of an item — attributed to a list-intonation template with penultimate/earlier prominence overriding the word pattern; in natural discourse (older speakers) the penultimate syllable of an intonation unit is prominent in listing clauses (p.106). Some TAME clitics shift the prominence of a verbal host; with nouns clitics leave the root pattern intact and are less prominent. /k/-deletion and vowel-string reduction at word boundaries can delete edge syllables, effect on prominence uninvestigated.
new_statements.domain_note: Observations are on isolated words from a word-list reading task by one speaker (Cecilio Teytaro), two repetitions each, analysed in Praat; citation forms. Clitic+host forms a phonological word with one primary-prominence syllable. Author states no morphosyntactic analysis in the grammar depends on stress and that word-level prominence 'interacts to a considerable extent with higher-level patterns of intonation'.
new_statements.identity_note: sana1281 'Sanapaná (Retired)' is a Glottolog bookkeeping entry for the pre-2014 ISO 639-3 code [sap], which ISO CR 2013-013 (downloaded, read) split into Sanapaná [spn] = Glottolog sana1298 and Angaité [aqt] = anga1316 because the two are not mutually intelligible. The stress statement quoted here (Van Gysel 2024; corroborated by Silva Gomes 2013) describes Sanapaná proper = sana1298, which per is ALREADY in the catalog ('well-sourced', 'confirmed in the copy we hold') from exactly this source. Adding sana1281 would double-count one language under a retired code; it should be mapped to sana1298 (and, for the Angaité half, to anga1316, for which no stress description is known), not catalogued separately.

new_statements.quote: If the tress [sic] in Spanish loans is maintained and results therefore in an abnormal position for Sanapaná (i.e. preceding the last syllable), this is indicated by means of an acute accent on the stressed syllable. In this case, stress is adapted to the Sanapaná system (vak’ka). [fn.2, p.27] || ’ stress lies on the next syllable [abbreviations, p.xii] || The Sanapaná particles, on the other hand, can never be independent phonetic words. Instead, they always encliticise to the preceding word, forming together one phonetic unit. In this process, stress shifts away from the root and onto the clitic: as such, forms such as enenta:men’aɬta (from enen’ta:men ‘past’), keɬwoje’ɬke (from keɬwo’je ‘moment’) and pesa:sepha’ta (from pe’sa:sep) are created. [pp.47-48]

new_statements.relation_note: Language not in the catalog under this retired code; the existing statement (Van Gysel 2024 diss., sec. 3.4.1: second syllable of bisyllabic nouns most prominent, pitch the main correlate) is final placement, and the 2017 footnote's 'abnormal position.. preceding the last syllable' presupposes the same final-syllable norm. It adds detail on loan adaptation and on clitic groups. Small tension: 2017 says stress shifts from root onto the enclitic particle; the 2024 dissertation (pp.158-160) finds noun roots keep their prominence under cliticisation and the clitic is less prominent in 5 of 8 noun tokens, more variable with verbs. The 2017 long-vowel-penult forms (enen'ta:men, pe'sa:sep, a trisy…
new_statements.rule_in_words: Word stress normally falls on the last syllable; a penultimate stress position is 'abnormal' for Sanapaná and occurs only in Spanish loans that keep their source stress (marked with an acute accent, e.g. mésa 'table' p.31, eskwéla, domíŋgo, lúnes p.44), otherwise the loan is adapted to final stress (vak'ka 'cow'). When the temporal particles aɬta, ɬke, hata encliticise, stress moves off the root onto the clitic, i.e. stays at the right edge of the phonological word (enenta:men'aɬta, keɬwoje'ɬke, pesa:sepha'ta). The thesis has no dedicated stress section; the placement rule is stated only implicitly in the footnote and in the notation convention. Note that two of the three cited base forms are marked with stress on a long-vowelled penult (enen'ta:men, pe'sa:sep) while keɬwo'je is final; the author does not comment on this, so a possible long-vowel attraction is an unstated observation, not a rule of the source.
new_statements.exceptions: Spanish loans that retain penultimate stress (written with acute accent); stress shift onto enclitic temporal particles; the marked forms enen'ta:men and pe'sa:sep show stress on the long-vowel penult rather than the final syllable, uncommented.
new_statements.identity_note: sana1281 is a retired bookkeeping code (old ISO [sap]), split in 2014 into Sanapaná sana1298 and Angaité anga1316 (ISO 639-3 change request 2013-013, already held by the project in our files). Van Gysel 2017 describes Sanapaná proper as spoken in La Esperanza (Paraguayan Chaco), i.e. sana1298, from the author's 2016-2017 fieldwork; the comparative chapter also cites Enlhet, Enxet, Guaná, Enenlhet and Angaité data from other sources but makes no stress statement about them. Nothing here describes Angaité stress.

readall_conflicts: No disagreement on placement: both Van Gysel 2017 (MA thesis, footnote 2 p.27 and notation p.xii) and the already-recorded Van Gysel 2024 dissertation put the normal Sanapaná prominence on the last syllable, with Spanish loans keeping penultimate stress as the marked exception. Two second-order tensions, both within the same author's work and both unresolved by 2017 itself: (1) 2017 states that stress shifts from the root onto an encliticised temporal particle, whereas 2024's acoustic pilot finds the root keeps its prominence and the clitic is usually less prominent for nouns (5/8 tokens) and variable for verbs; (2) two of the three stress-marked 2017 base forms carry the mark on a long-vowelled penult (enen'ta:men 'past', pe'sa:sep 'night') rather than the final syllable, which 2017 does not explain and 2024 (final prominence in trisyllabic nouns, though with token-to-token variation) does not confirm. The 2024 dissertation, being the later and instrumentally based description, is the better source; the 2017 material is impressionistic and the author says he 'did not focus on phonology' (p.30).
